summary: Defines registration procedures for message header fields used by Internet mail, HTTP, Netnews and other applications. It creates a common place to record headers and the rules for adding new ones. It is a Best Current Practice.

eli5.summary: Names for the labels on messages get written in one official list. This document says how to add a new label name to it.

questions: how to register a new message header
how to register a message header field
what is the iana message headers registry
subtitle: How message header field names for mail, HTTP and netnews get recorded in IANA registries.

tldr.problem: Header field names are used by Internet mail, HTTP, Netnews and other applications, and without a shared list the same name can be defined twice for different purposes.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC creates a Permanent Message Header Field Registry for headers with a published specification and a Provisional repository for any citable proposal, with templates and a submission procedure.
tldr.outcome: Developers get one place to look up header names and their defining documents. RFC 9110 later updated this RFC.

facts.label: Discussion period before sending to IANA

today: RFC 3864 is a Best Current Practice. It has not been obsoleted, but it has been updated by RFC 9110.

sections.title: Why a Header Registry
sections.content:
This specification defines registration procedures for message header field names used by Internet mail, HTTP, newsgroup feeds and other applications. It does not replace protocol-specific registries such as the SIP registry.

The RFC lists the benefits of a central registry: a single reference point for standardized and widely used names, easy discovery of defining documents, discouraging several definitions of one name, helping proposers avoid confusing names, and encouraging convergence across applications. The main specifications are the Internet mail format (RFC 2822), HTTP/1.0 and HTTP/1.1, and RFC 1036 for Netnews, along with MIME and related documents.

Applications such as mail to Netnews gateways exchange messages with each other, so a common reference reduces accidental collisions.
sections.eli5: Many programs put labels on messages. One shared list of label names keeps two programs from using the same name for different things.

sections.title: Permanent and Provisional Fields
sections.content:
Some header fields come from standards-track documents, some are experimental, and many are ad hoc names that spread through use. To cover all of these while keeping a clear status for those with community consensus, the RFC defines two repositories.

  • The Permanent Message Header Field Registry is for headers defined in IETF standards-track documents, those with comparable review, or those generally recognized as widespread. The policy is "Specification Required" from RFC 2434, and the specification must be an RFC or an Open Standard in the sense of RFC 2026, section 7.
  • The Provisional Message Header Field Repository is for any header proposed by any developer, with no claim about its quality. The policy is "Private Use".

Neither repository records syntax, semantics or the type of values. Only the field name, applicable protocol and status are registered, and everything else lives in the defining documents.
sections.eli5: There are two lists. One is for names that were properly written up and checked. The other is a sign-up sheet where anyone can post a name they want to use.

sections.title: Protocols, MIME and Name Reuse
sections.content:
The same field name may be specified differently for different protocols. For example, the Date header used with HTTP has a different syntax from the Date header in Internet mail. So each registered header names the protocol it applies to. A name may have several entries for different protocols, but in the Permanent registry it may be registered only once per protocol.

MIME header fields with names of the form Content-* can be applied to a data object separately from the protocol carrying it. They are registered with the protocol "mime" and are presumed usable with any protocol that conveys MIME objects. HTTP has similar fields that must be registered separately for HTTP.

The RFC calls it poor practice to reuse a header name from another protocol just because the meanings are similar. Protocols should share names only when meanings are identical in all foreseeable circumstances.
sections.eli5: The same label can mean slightly different things in different places, so each entry says which place it is for. Do not borrow a name unless it means exactly the same thing.

sections.title: How to Register a Header
sections.content:
Registration has three steps: construct a header field specification, prepare a registration template, and submit it. RFCs that define new headers for Internet mail, HTTP or MIME MUST include the registration templates in their IANA considerations section. Otherwise use of the registry is not required unless another specification mandates it.

A registered name SHOULD conform at least to the syntax in RFC 2822, section 3.6.8. The "." character is reserved to indicate a naming sub-structure and MUST NOT appear in a registered name. For maximum flexibility, names SHOULD be limited to letters, digits, hyphen and underscore, with a first character that is a letter or underscore.

Both templates ask for the header field name, applicable protocol ("mail", "mime", "http", "netnews" or another standards-track protocol), status, author or change controller, specification documents and optional related information. A Permanent header MUST be published as an RFC or Open Standard and have a name unique for its protocol. A Provisional header MUST have a citable specification and no matching Permanent entry, and its status is "provisional".
sections.eli5: To get a name on the list you fill in a form saying the name, what it is for, who owns it and where it is explained. The name should use only simple letters, digits, dashes and underscores.

sections.title: Submission, Objections and Change Control
sections.content:
A template can be submitted in two ways: through an IANA considerations section in a defining RFC, or by sending it to the designated email discussion list, waiting at least 2 weeks for comments, and then sending it to IANA. When a name enters the Permanent registry, IANA removes the matching Provisional entry.

Provisional listings should not be lightly refused. Grounds can include likely harm to Internet infrastructure by IETF consensus, frivolous use, a proposal lacking purpose, or conflict with current IETF activity. Technical disagreement alone is not grounds. The IESG nominates a designated expert to confirm to IANA that criteria are met, and the IESG is the final arbiter of any objection.

Changes to Permanent entries follow the same conditions as the first registration. IANA MAY remove a Provisional entry whose specification is no longer available, after contacting the author. Once a Permanent entry exists, the name and protocol pair MUST NOT be registered for any other purpose, because entries may be used to build URNs that need uniqueness and persistence.
sections.eli5: A helper checks that the form is filled in properly, and the names are only turned down for good reasons. Once a name is in the main list, nobody else can ever use it for something different.

sections.title: IANA and Security Considerations
sections.content:
The IANA section calls for a new registry for permanent message header fields, a new repository for provisional ones, and an IESG-appointed designated expert. No initial entries are provided.

The security section says no security considerations are introduced beyond those already inherent in the use of message headers.
sections.eli5: The lists start out empty, and having them does not add any new danger.
